titleEn: Do not cast me off in old age
progression: | Dm Dm | Gm Gm | Bb C | Dm Dm |
intro: Twenty-four verses in the voice of someone who has already lived a long time and is asking not to be dropped at the end of it. The Hebrew gives this psalm no heading at all, which is unusual in this part of the book, and its first verse is identical to the opening line of Psalm 31, with the two verses after it reworking the same material more loosely. Three roots carry the argument: shame in verses 1, 13 and 24, abandon in 9, 11 and 18, and the word for always in 3, 6 and 14. In the thirty-day reading cycle it falls on the thirteenth day.

stichs.en: In You, LORD, I have taken refuge;
let me never be ashamed.

verses.summary: The verb is already in the past tense: refuge was taken before any trouble is described. The only request is that the choice not turn out to have been a mistake.

stichs.en: In Your righteousness rescue me and set me free;
turn Your ear toward me and save me.

verses.summary: Four imperatives in one breath, three of them carrying the object suffix meaning me. The rescue is asked for on the basis of God's righteousness, not the speaker's.

stichs.en: Be for me a rock of refuge, to come to always;
You have given the order to save me,
for You are my crag and my fortress.

verses.summary: A rock is a place you reach, so what is asked for is a standing right of entry rather than one deliverance. The last clause quietly turns the request into a statement of fact.

stichs.en: My God, set me free from the hand of a wicked man,
from the grip of the unjust and the ruthless.

verses.summary: The first mention of the enemy, and it stays generic: a hand, a palm, no name. The threat is identified by what it does rather than by who it is.

stichs.en: For You are my hope,
Lord GOD, my trust since my youth.

verses.summary: The ground shifts from what God should do to how long He has already been doing it. Youth enters the psalm here and does not leave it.

stichs.en: Upon You I have leaned since birth;
from my mother's body You are the one who brought me out;
my praise is of You always.

glosses: are the one who brought me out
verses.summary: Dependence is pushed back behind memory, to the womb. If leaning on God is the oldest fact about him, being dropped now would break something older than the present trouble.

stichs.en: I have become a portent to many,
but You are my strong refuge.

verses.summary: A portent is something people stare at and read as a sign, and it can point either to favour or to disaster. He knows he is being read as a public case.

stichs.en: Let my mouth be filled with Your praise,
all the day with Your splendour.

verses.summary: The answer to being stared at is not silence but speech: fill the mouth the others are watching. Praise here is a way of occupying the whole day.

stichs.en: Do not throw me away at the time of old age;
when my strength runs out, do not abandon me.

verses.summary: The psalm's central fear, said twice in one verse with two different verbs. Old age is not described as weakness in general but as the point where strength runs out mid-sentence.

stichs.en: For my enemies have talked about me,
and those who watch for my life have taken counsel together,

verses.summary: The enemies get their own verse and their own meeting. They are watching him closely, which makes them the exact mirror of the God he is asking not to look away.

stichs.en: saying, God has abandoned him;
chase him down and seize him,
for there is no one to rescue.

verses.summary: Their logic quoted in their own words: they read his suffering as proof of abandonment. Their verb for abandon is the same one he uses in his own prayer.

stichs.en: God, do not stay far from me;
my God, hurry to help me.

verses.summary: The prayer cuts back in on top of the accusation. Two names of God in one short verse, and the request has narrowed from rescue to nearness and speed.

stichs.en: Let the accusers of my life be shamed and finished;
let those who seek my harm be wrapped in disgrace and humiliation.

verses.summary: The counter-petition. What he asked not to suffer in verse 1 is what he asks be laid on them, and it is described as a garment they put on.

stichs.en: But as for me, I will keep waiting,
and I will add to all Your praise.

verses.summary: The hinge of the whole psalm. Against their counsel he sets one word, always, and against their pursuit one act, adding more praise.

stichs.en: My mouth will recount Your righteousness,
all the day Your salvation,
for I do not know their number.

verses.summary: Counting is the subject: he will tell what God has done and admits in the same breath that he cannot reach the end of the sum.

stichs.en: I will come with the mighty acts of the Lord GOD;
I will bring to mind Your righteousness, Yours alone.

verses.summary: The mighty acts belong to God, and he arrives carrying them the way a witness arrives carrying evidence. The last word insists the record is nobody else's.

stichs.en: God, You have taught me since my youth,
and until now I declare Your wonders.

verses.summary: Youth comes back, this time as the start of an education rather than of trust. Everything from then to this moment is presented as one unbroken stretch of teaching.

stichs.en: And even to old age and grey hair, God, do not abandon me,
until I declare Your arm to a generation,
Your might to all who are to come.

verses.summary: The longest verse, and the one that gives a reason for wanting more years: not comfort but handover. He wants to stay alive long enough to pass something on.

stichs.en: And Your righteousness, God, reaches to the height,
You who have done great things,
God, who is like You?

verses.summary: The prayer stops asking and looks upward. The closing question is not rhetoric filling a line; it is what the two verses about teaching were building toward.

stichs.en: You who have made me see many hard troubles,
You will give me life again,
and from the depths of the earth You will bring me up again.

verses.summary: The troubles are put down to God as directly as the rescue is. Two verbs of returning frame the verse: whatever went down is expected back up.

stichs.en: You will increase my greatness,
and turn and comfort me.

verses.summary: The shortest verse here, and the only one with no enemy, no fear and no argument in it. Four words, all of them things done to him.

stichs.en: I too will thank You with the lute for Your faithfulness, my God;
I will sing to You with the lyre, Holy One of Israel.

verses.summary: The instruments arrive. Thanks are tied to one specific attribute, faithfulness, which is the one that matters when a case has been running for decades.

stichs.en: My lips will ring out when I sing to You,
and my soul, which You have redeemed.

verses.summary: The body takes over from the argument: lips first, then the soul, both named as the parts that make the sound. Redemption is stated as already done.

stichs.en: My tongue too will speak of Your righteousness all the day,
for those who seek my harm are shamed and disgraced.

verses.summary: The last verse holds both halves at once, his speech all day long and their shame, and closes the psalm on the same root that opened it.

pardes.body: An old man's petition, in four movements. Verses 1 to 3 are the opening appeal, and they are not new: verse 1 is word for word the opening line of Psalm 31, and the next two reuse its vocabulary of rescue, ear, rock and fortress in a different order, so the appeal reads like a formula being invoked rather than a sentence being invented. Verses 4 to 13 are the crisis, with the specific fear stated in {{9.1}} and repeated at {{18.6}}: not death, but being put down like something no longer worth carrying. Verse 14 is the hinge, and everything after it is praise, promise and instruments. The word to track is the one for always, which lands three times, at {{3.5}}, {{6.9}} and {{14.1}}, each time attached to something the speaker does rather than something he receives.

The psalm is built on one root, the root of shame, and the plot is which way it points. In {{1.4}} he asks not to be shamed; in {{13.0}} he asks that his accusers be; in {{24.7}} they are. Nothing else in the psalm is resolved that cleanly. A second root does the same work in the opposite direction: the enemies say in {{11.2}} that God has abandoned him, and he uses their verb in his own request at {{18.6}}, so their taunt and his prayer are the same word with the subject changed. The one genuinely obscure word is {{6.6}}. Translations render it as the one who took me from the womb, but the verb is rare and its root is disputed, and the meaning here is reconstructed from the birth imagery around it rather than from parallel usage.

Read verse 18 as the psalm's real request and the whole thing changes shape. He does not ask for more years so that the years will be pleasant; he asks for enough time to declare God's arm to a generation that has not yet arrived, which makes length of days an obligation rather than a reward. On that reading the fear in verse 9 is not fear of dying but fear of being made irrelevant before the handover is complete. There is also the long standing habit of reading the psalms of the single sufferer as the voice of the whole people, and this one takes it easily: a nation held since the womb, told by onlookers in verse 11 that it has been abandoned, asking in verse 20 to be brought up again from the depths of the earth.

Two places in this psalm sit below the surface of the ground, and they answer each other. In {{6.3}} the speaker comes out of his mother's body; in {{20.7}} he is brought back up from the depths of the earth. Between them, verse 20 uses the same verb twice, at {{20.5}} and {{20.9}}, a verb of returning that turns both the reviving and the raising into a coming back rather than a first arrival. Later Jewish mysticism states the pattern as a rule, that the descent is for the sake of the ascent, and the verse supplies the grammar for it: the trouble is credited to God in the same breath as the rescue, one clause apart, with no attempt to separate the two hands.
